title: discord.py: Building Discord Bots
subtitle: Clients, intents, commands, cogs, slash commands, views, modals, tasks and deployment, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on course based on the open-source discord.py library (github.com/Rapptz/discord.py, MIT), documented here as of its 2.8.0a development version. Learn how a bot connects, which intents it needs, how prefix and slash commands work, how to organise code with cogs and extensions, build buttons, selects and modals, run background tasks, log and handle errors, and keep tokens and permissions safe. Labs run offline and simulate the library's rules in Python, so no Discord account is needed.

chapters.title: The client, events and the gateway

maps.title: discord.py basics
links: on_ready | fires after | Cache is filled

summary: discord.py is an asynchronous Python library for the Discord API. You create a Client, give it intents, register event handlers, and call run with your bot token.
The client keeps a websocket connection, called the gateway, open to Discord. Discord pushes events down it, such as a message being sent, and the library calls your matching coroutine.
The repository at github.com/Rapptz/discord.py was at version 2.8.0a in its development branch when this course was written. The quickstart says to avoid naming your own file discord.py.

glossary.def: The object that connects to Discord and dispatches events to your handlers.
The websocket connection over which Discord pushes events to the bot.
An async function named on_<event>, registered with client.event.
A function defined with async def, run by the event loop and paused with await.
A 64-bit id used for users, guilds, channels and messages; its top bits hold a timestamp.

keyPoints: Create intents, then Client(intents=intents), then client.run(token).
Handlers are coroutines named on_ready, on_message and so on.
Always ignore your own messages so the bot does not reply to itself.
Never name your script discord.py.
Snowflake time = (id >> 22) + 1420070400000 milliseconds.

items: ELI5. Your bot is a kid with a walkie-talkie. Discord talks on it all day, and the kid only answers the messages it was told to listen for.

Think of the bot as a person sitting by a telephone. The Client dials Discord once and keeps the line open. Whenever something happens in a server, Discord speaks down the line, and the library turns each sentence into a call to one of your functions.

Your functions are coroutines. They are defined with async def, and they pause with await when they need to wait for the network, so one bot can handle many events at once on a single thread without blocking.

lesson.code:
import discord

intents = discord.Intents.default()
intents.message_content = True

client = discord.Client(intents=intents)

@client.event
async def on_ready():
    print('Logged on as', client.user)

@client.event
async def on_message(message):
    if message.author == client.user:
        return
    if message.content.startswith('$hello'):
        await message.channel.send('Hello!')

client.run('your token here')

items: This is the quickstart bot. The first lines build the intents, the next create the client, and the two decorated functions are event handlers. The check on the author matters: without it the bot could answer its own replies forever.

on_ready fires once the client has logged in and filled its cache, but it can fire more than once after reconnects, so do not start one-time work there. A later chapter shows setup_hook, which runs exactly once.

Every id in Discord is a snowflake. The top bits are the number of milliseconds since the Discord epoch, 1 January 2015, so you can read when something was created from its id alone. Shift right by 22 bits and add the epoch.

chapters.title: Intents and the developer portal
summary: Intents tell Discord which groups of events your bot wants. Fewer intents mean less data, less memory, and fewer events to process.
Three intents are privileged: presences, members and message_content. You must switch each on in the Bot tab of the developer portal and also enable it in code. Enabling only one side fails.
Bots in more than 100 guilds need verification and approval before they can use privileged intents. Intents.default() turns on everything except the privileged three.

glossary.def: Flags that choose which events Discord sends to the bot.
An intent that must be enabled in the developer portal: presences, members, message content.
The library's stored copy of guild members; controlled by the members intent and MemberCacheFlags.
The Discord website where you create the application, the bot user and its token.
Discord's review required once a bot is in more than 100 guilds.

keyPoints: Intents.default() leaves out presences, members and message_content.
Privileged intents need the portal toggle and the code flag.
Without message_content, message.content is empty for most messages.
Intents.none() plus the ones you need is the leanest start.
Over 100 guilds: apply for verification.

items: ELI5. Intents are like choosing which TV channels you get. The grown-up has to say yes to the three special channels first.

Imagine a mailroom that sorts mail into bins. Intents are the bins you ask to receive. If you ask only for guild messages and guild changes, the mailroom never sends you reactions, typing notices or member updates. That saves your bot work and saves Discord bandwidth.

Three bins hold sensitive material. presences shows who is online and what they are playing, members shows join and leave events and fills the member list, and message_content lets you read the text of messages. These are privileged, which means a person must approve them.

lesson.code:
import discord

intents = discord.Intents.none()
intents.guilds = True
intents.guild_messages = True
intents.message_content = True   # also enable in the portal

# or start from the default set
intents = discord.Intents.default()
intents.members = True           # privileged

client = discord.Client(intents=intents)

items: If you forget the portal switch the bot fails to connect with a privileged intents error. If you forget the code flag, events silently never arrive. When on_message fires but message.content is empty, the cause is nearly always a missing message_content intent.

The member cache needs the members intent. Without it the library cannot list everyone, but the author of a message is still given as a Member, built from the data in the message itself. You can narrow what is cached with MemberCacheFlags.
Choose intents from the events you handle. A moderation bot wants members and message_content; a slash command bot often needs neither, because interactions arrive without them.

chapters.title: commands.Bot and prefix commands
summary: The commands extension adds a Bot class that extends Client with a command system. Messages that start with a prefix are parsed into a command name and arguments.
Each command is a coroutine whose first parameter is a Context. Annotations such as int or discord.Member convert the text arguments for you, and checks decide who may run the command.
Errors raised by conversion or checks arrive in an error handler as subclasses of CommandError, so you can answer with a friendly message instead of a traceback.

glossary.def: A Client subclass from discord.ext.commands that parses commands from messages.
An object passed to a command holding the message, author, channel and a send method.
A type annotation or class that turns an argument string into a Python object.
A predicate that must pass before a command runs, such as has_permissions.
A limit on how often a command may be used.

keyPoints: commands.Bot(command_prefix='!', intents=intents).
A command is async def name(ctx, ...) with @bot.command().
Quote arguments with spaces: !say "hello world".
Annotations convert: int, float, discord.Member, discord.TextChannel.
Handle on_command_error for BadArgument and MissingPermissions.

items: ELI5. A prefix command is like a secret word at the start of a sentence. If a sentence starts with the secret word, the bot knows you are talking to it.

The Bot class does the parsing a person would do by hand. It watches every message, checks whether it begins with your prefix, splits off the command name, then splits the rest into arguments, respecting quotation marks.

lesson.code:
import discord
from discord.ext import commands

intents = discord.Intents.default()
intents.message_content = True
bot = commands.Bot(command_prefix='!', intents=intents)

@bot.command()
async def add(ctx, a: int, b: int):
    await ctx.send(str(a + b))

@bot.command()
@commands.has_permissions(kick_members=True)
async def warn(ctx, member: discord.Member, *, reason: str):
    await ctx.send(member.display_name + ' warned: ' + reason)

bot.run('token')

items: In add, the annotations int make the library convert both arguments, and if the text is not a number it raises BadArgument. In warn, a bare star means the last parameter swallows the rest of the message as one string, so reasons can contain spaces.

Checks are decorators. has_permissions tests the author's permissions, is_owner tests the bot owner, and cooldown limits use. A failed check raises a CommandError that you can catch in one central handler.

A prefix can be a list or a function, and commands.when_mentioned_or('!') lets people either type the prefix or mention the bot. Because prefix commands read message text, they depend on the message_content intent, which is why many new bots prefer slash commands.

chapters.title: Cogs, extensions and setup_hook

maps.title: Structure
links: Extension | is | A module with setup
Listener | handles | Events in a cog

summary: As a bot grows, one file becomes unmanageable. Cogs are classes that group related commands and listeners, and extensions are modules that can be loaded, unloaded and reloaded while the bot runs.
An extension defines an async setup function that receives the bot and adds cogs. You load it with bot.load_extension('cogs.fun'), usually inside setup_hook, which runs once before the bot connects.
Reloading an extension picks up new code without a restart, which makes development fast. A cog may also define cog-wide checks and an error handler.

glossary.def: A class deriving from commands.Cog that groups commands, listeners and state.
A Python module with a setup function that registers cogs on the bot.
A coroutine on the Client or Bot that runs once, before connecting, ideal for loading extensions.
A method in a cog decorated with commands.Cog.listener() that handles an event.
Unload and load an extension again to apply edited code.

keyPoints: class Fun(commands.Cog) holds commands; add it with await bot.add_cog(Fun(bot)).
Extension file defines async def setup(bot).
Load in setup_hook: await self.load_extension('cogs.fun').
Use @commands.Cog.listener() for events inside cogs.
load, unload and reload raise errors if already or not loaded.

items: ELI5. A cog is a toy box for one game. The bot has many boxes, and you can take one out and put a fixed one back in without stopping the whole party.

Picture a shop where every department has its own team. A cog is one team: it owns some commands, some event listeners and any state they share, such as a counter. The bot is the shop that hires the teams.

lesson.code:
# cogs/fun.py
from discord.ext import commands

class Fun(commands.Cog):
    def __init__(self, bot):
        self.bot = bot
        self.count = 0

    @commands.command()
    async def ping(self, ctx):
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.send('pong %d' % self.count)

    @commands.Cog.listener()
    async def on_member_join(self, member):
        print('welcome', member)

async def setup(bot):
    await bot.add_cog(Fun(bot))

items: Inside a cog, commands take self first and then ctx. Events use the Cog.listener decorator instead of client.event, so many cogs can listen to the same event without replacing one another.

setup_hook runs once, before the websocket connects, so it is the right place to load extensions, open a database or start background tasks. on_ready is the wrong place for those because it can fire again after a reconnect.

While developing, call await bot.reload_extension('cogs.fun') from an owner-only command. Loading a name twice raises ExtensionAlreadyLoaded, and unloading one that is not loaded raises ExtensionNotLoaded.

chapters.title: Slash commands and the command tree

maps.title: Application commands
links: Global sync | takes | Up to an hour

summary: Slash commands are registered with Discord, so users see them in a menu with descriptions and typed options. They arrive as interactions, not as messages, so they need no message content intent.

You keep them in an app_commands.CommandTree, decorate functions with tree.command, and call tree.sync to publish them. Syncing to one test guild is instant, while global commands can take up to an hour to appear.
Your handler receives an Interaction. You must respond within three seconds, either with response.send_message, or by deferring first if the work takes longer.

glossary.def: The container that stores and syncs application commands.
The object received for a slash command, button or modal; used to respond.
Sending the command definitions to Discord so they appear to users.
Telling Discord you need more time; you then answer with a followup.
A response visible only to the user who triggered it.

keyPoints: Create self.tree = app_commands.CommandTree(self) in your Client.
Sync in setup_hook: copy_global_to(guild=...), then sync(guild=...).
Respond to an interaction within 3 seconds.
Use describe and rename for friendly options.
Use ephemeral=True for private replies.

items: ELI5. A slash command is a form with blanks that Discord draws for you, so you cannot write a silly answer in the wrong box.

A prefix command is plain chat text that the bot reads. A slash command is a form that Discord itself draws. Discord checks the options before your code runs, so you get typed values, and users get autocomplete for free.

lesson.code:
import discord
from discord import app_commands

MY_GUILD = discord.Object(id=0)  # replace with your guild id

class MyClient(discord.Client):
    def __init__(self, *, intents):
        super().__init__(intents=intents)
        self.tree = app_commands.CommandTree(self)

    async def setup_hook(self):
        self.tree.copy_global_to(guild=MY_GUILD)
        await self.tree.sync(guild=MY_GUILD)

client = MyClient(intents=discord.Intents.default())

@client.tree.command()
@app_commands.describe(first='The first value', second='The second value')
async def add(interaction: discord.Interaction, first: int, second: int):
    await interaction.response.send_message(str(first + second))

items: This follows the project's own example. Copying the global commands to your test guild and syncing there makes changes appear immediately, which is the way to develop. For release you sync globally and wait.

The type hints define the option types. A parameter with a default of None, or annotated Optional, becomes an optional option. Required options must come before optional ones, and descriptions are limited to 100 characters.

lesson.code:
@client.tree.command()
async def slow(interaction: discord.Interaction):
    await interaction.response.defer(ephemeral=True)
    # ... work that takes a while ...
    await interaction.followup.send('Done!')

items: If you do not respond within three seconds Discord shows the user that the application did not respond. Calling defer buys up to fifteen minutes, after which you send the real answer with followup.send.

chapters.title: Views, buttons and select menus
summary: A View is a container for interactive components such as buttons and select menus. You attach it to a message, and each component calls one of your coroutines when a user presses it.

Views time out after 180 seconds by default, after which the buttons stop working. A persistent view sets timeout to None, gives every item a custom_id and is registered at startup so it survives restarts.
Discord limits a message to five rows with five buttons each, so at most 25 buttons, and a select menu takes a whole row.

glossary.def: A discord.ui.View: a set of components attached to one message.
A clickable component declared with the discord.ui.button decorator.
A dropdown menu component with up to 25 options.
A string of up to 100 characters that identifies a component across restarts.
A view with timeout None and fixed custom ids, re-registered when the bot starts.

keyPoints: Subclass discord.ui.View and decorate methods with discord.ui.button.
Handler signature: (self, interaction, button).
Respond with interaction.response.edit_message(view=self).
Default timeout is 180 seconds; use None plus custom_id for persistence.
Maximum 25 buttons: five rows of five.

items: ELI5. A button on a message is a little remote control. If nobody uses it for a while the remote goes to sleep, unless you give it a special name tag.

A message can carry little controls, like a remote control stuck to it. In discord.py each control is a component and the whole set is a View. When someone presses a button Discord sends an interaction, and the library calls the method you decorated.

This mirrors the project's counter example. The button changes its own label, and edit_message redraws the message with the updated view. Notice that the button is a parameter, so the same method can change its own style and label.

A view only lives as long as the bot's memory and its timeout. When the timeout passes, on_timeout is called and the buttons stop responding. For menus that must live forever, give timeout=None, set a custom_id on each item and call bot.add_view in setup_hook.
Use interaction_check to limit who may press: return False for anyone except the person who started the command. That stops other users from confirming someone else's action.

Layout is automatic, filling rows left to right, but you can set row explicitly. A select menu occupies a full row, so a message can hold five selects, or four selects and a row of buttons, up to five rows in total.

chapters.title: Modals, embeds and message limits
summary: A Modal is a popup form. You declare TextInput fields on a class, show the modal in response to an interaction, and receive the typed answers in on_submit.

An Embed is a formatted card with a title, description, fields, colour and footer. Discord limits sizes: a description up to 4096 characters, field values up to 1024, a footer up to 2048, at most 25 fields, and 6000 characters across the whole embed.
Ordinary message text is limited to 2000 characters, so long output must be split.

A modal field with a label, placeholder, style and length limits.
A rich card attached to a message.

keyPoints: Modal subclass with title and TextInput attributes.
Show it with interaction.response.send_modal(Feedback()).

Message text limit is 2000 characters.
A modal can only be opened from an interaction, not from a plain message.

items: ELI5. A modal is a pop-up worksheet. You fill in the boxes, press submit, and the bot reads all your answers at once. Messages and cards also have size limits, like a postcard.

A modal asks several questions at once. You write a class with one TextInput per question, and when the user presses submit Discord sends all the answers back together so your on_submit method can read them.

lesson.code:
import discord

class Feedback(discord.ui.Modal, title='Feedback'):
    name = discord.ui.TextInput(label='Name', placeholder='Your name here...')
    feedback = discord.ui.TextInput(
        label='What do you think?',
        style=discord.TextStyle.long,
        placeholder='Type your feedback here...',
        required=False,
        max_length=300)

    async def on_submit(self, interaction: discord.Interaction):
        await interaction.response.send_message('Thanks, %s!' % self.name.value, ephemeral=True)

# await interaction.response.send_modal(Feedback())

items: This follows the repository's modal example. Each TextInput is a class attribute, and after submission its value property holds what the person typed. Use max_length and required to validate on the client side.

lesson.code:
embed = discord.Embed(title='Server stats', description='Updated hourly', colour=discord.Colour.blurple())
embed.add_field(name='Members', value='120', inline=True)
embed.add_field(name='Online', value='34', inline=True)
embed.set_footer(text='Powered by discord.py')
await ctx.send(embed=embed)

items: Embeds are rejected if any limit is exceeded, and the total of all text across the embed may not pass 6000 characters. The library exposes len(embed) so you can check before sending.

Plain messages are limited to 2000 characters. To send longer text, split it at line breaks so no piece exceeds the limit, and send the pieces in order. Never split in the middle of a word if you can avoid it.

chapters.title: Background tasks, logging and error handling
summary: The tasks extension runs a coroutine on a fixed schedule, such as every 60 seconds. You start it in setup_hook and make it wait until the bot is ready before it touches channels.

discord.py uses the standard logging module. By default client.run sets up a handler and a level for you; you can pass your own log_handler and log_level, or pass log_handler=None to configure logging yourself.

Network calls fail in predictable ways. Forbidden means the bot lacks access, NotFound means the object is gone, and HTTPException covers other API errors. Retrying should back off instead of hammering Discord.

glossary.def: A decorator that repeats a coroutine on an interval.
A hook that runs before the loop begins, often awaiting wait_until_ready.
Python's standard logging; discord.py logs its gateway and HTTP activity under 'discord'.
The error raised when the bot lacks permission or access.
Waiting longer after each failed attempt.

keyPoints: @tasks.loop(seconds=60) repeats; start with .start() in setup_hook.
@loop.before_loop: await self.wait_until_ready().
client.run(token, log_handler=handler, log_level=logging.DEBUG).
log_handler=None disables the default setup.
Catch Forbidden, NotFound and HTTPException around API calls.

items: ELI5. A background task is a cuckoo clock: it does a job at the same time every minute. Waiting until the house is ready stops it from looking for a room that is not built yet.
Some jobs must happen on a schedule, such as posting a daily summary. The tasks extension wraps a coroutine in a loop that sleeps between runs and recovers from many transient errors for you.

lesson.code:
import discord
from discord.ext import tasks

class MyClient(discord.Client):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.counter = 0

    async def setup_hook(self):
        self.my_background_task.start()

    @tasks.loop(seconds=60)
    async def my_background_task(self):
        channel = self.get_channel(1234567)  # replace with a channel id
        self.counter += 1
        await channel.send(str(self.counter))

    @my_background_task.before_loop
    async def before_my_task(self):
        await self.wait_until_ready()

items: This is the project's background task example. before_loop waits until the cache is ready, because get_channel returns None until the guilds are loaded. Also remember that a loop keeps running until you call cancel on it.

lesson.code:
import logging
handler = logging.FileHandler(filename='discord.log', encoding='utf-8', mode='w')
client.run(token, log_handler=handler, log_level=logging.DEBUG)

items: The documentation also describes discord.utils.setup_logging for use when you do not call run, and a root_logger option if you want your own modules to share the same handler. Raise the level to DEBUG while diagnosing a problem.

When an API call fails, catch the narrowest error you can. Forbidden means fix permissions, not retry. For a transient HTTPException, wait, double the wait on each failure, cap it, and give up after a few tries.

practice.title: Backoff schedule
practice.intro: Write backoff(attempts, base, cap): return the list of waits for that many retries; the first wait is base, each next doubles, and no wait exceeds cap.
practice.solution:
def backoff(attempts, base, cap):
    out = []
    w = base
    for i in range(attempts):
        out.append(min(w, cap))
        w = w * 2
    return out

chapters.title: Permissions, tokens and deployment
summary: Your bot token is a password. Anyone who has it can act as your bot. Keep it out of source control and out of screenshots, and read it from an environment variable or a secrets file.

Discord permissions are bit flags combined in one integer. Administrator overrides all of the others. Ask for the minimum your bot needs when you generate the invite link, and check the bot's own permissions before you act.
If a token leaks, regenerate it in the developer portal at once. A deployed bot needs a process manager or container that restarts it after a crash and keeps logs.

glossary.def: The secret string that logs your bot in.
An integer where each bit is one permission.
Granting only the permissions the bot needs.
A process setting used to pass secrets without writing them in code.
A tool such as systemd or a container runtime that restarts the bot.

keyPoints: Never hardcode or commit the token; read it from the environment.
If it leaks, reset it in the developer portal immediately.
Permissions are bits: administrator is 1 << 3, send_messages 1 << 11.
Administrator overrides every other permission.
Run under a supervisor with logs and a restart policy.

items: ELI5. The token is your bot's secret password. Anyone with it can pretend to be your bot, so you keep it in a locked drawer, never taped to the front door.

A token is like the key to a building. If it is pasted into a public repository, bots scan for it within minutes and use it. Discord scans too and may reset leaked tokens, but do not rely on that. Treat the token like a password.

lesson.code:
import os
import discord

token = os.environ['DISCORD_TOKEN']
intents = discord.Intents.default()
client = discord.Client(intents=intents)
client.run(token)

# shell:
#   export DISCORD_TOKEN='...'
#   python bot.py

items: Add your .env file or secrets file to .gitignore, and keep a template without values in the repository. If the token ever appears in a log, a chat message or a commit, reset it and update the deployment.

Permissions are an integer where each bit is one capability, for example kick_members is bit one, administrator is bit three, view_channel is bit ten, send_messages is bit eleven and manage_messages is bit thirteen. You test one with a bitwise and.

Request only what you use. A music bot needs to connect and speak, not to ban members. When a command acts on a member, also check that the bot's role is above the target's role, or Discord will refuse with Forbidden.

In production run the bot under systemd, Docker or a hosting platform that restarts it and captures logs. Handle signals so it can close cleanly, and monitor for repeated reconnects, which can mean rate limits or a bad token.
